title: How to Build a Career Plan That Survives Change
excerpt: Job titles change faster than any ten-year plan can track. Learn how to plan around skills instead, run an honest skills audit, and work in 90-day cycles that keep your career moving no matter what the market does.
content:
A few years ago I sat with a mentee in Nairobi, let's call her Wanjiru, while she walked me through her career plan. It was beautiful. One page, ten years: senior analyst by 2022, product manager by 2025, head of product by 2029.

Eighteen months later her company restructured. The product team was dissolved. The exact title she had been climbing toward stopped existing at her firm. Her plan didn't bend. It snapped.

Here's the part worth remembering. Wanjiru recovered quickly, and not because she found another ladder. She stopped planning around job titles and started planning around skills. Today she leads customer research at a fintech serving Lagos and Nairobi, a role that appeared nowhere on her original page.

That switch, from title-based planning to skills-based planning, is the most useful career decision you can make this year. Let me show you how to do it.

Why plans built on job titles keep breaking

The old advice was simple. Pick a destination job, list the promotions between here and there, then climb. It assumed the ladder would hold still long enough for you to reach the top.

It won't. Employers now expect 39 percent of workers' core skills to change by 2030, according to the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025. LinkedIn's researchers go further: they estimate that 70 percent of the skills used in most jobs will change by 2030, with AI doing much of the pushing. People entering the workforce today are also on track to hold twice as many jobs over their careers as those who started 15 years ago.

For young Africans the pressure is doubled. The ILO and the African Development Bank estimate that 10 to 12 million young Africans enter the labour market every year, competing for roughly three million formal jobs. When titles are that scarce and that unstable, betting your whole future on one of them is a risk you don't need to take.

We've written about the bigger shift in The New World of Work Is Already Here. The short version: change is not an interruption to your career. It is the weather your career happens in.

Career capital: the asset that survives the storm

So what should you plan around instead? Career capital.

Career capital is the stock of rare and valuable things you carry with you when a job disappears: skills people pay for, work you can show, and people who will vouch for you. A title belongs to your employer. Career capital belongs to you.

Think of an audit senior in Accra who learns data analysis on the side. If her firm downsizes, the title stays behind. The financial models, the dashboards, and the partner willing to recommend her all travel with her. That's the difference between losing a job and losing a career.

The framework below is how you build that kind of portability on purpose.

The framework: six steps, repeated every 90 days

  1. Aim at problems, not positions. Write one sentence describing the problems you want to be paid to solve in five years, without using a job title. "I help businesses collect payments across borders" survives a restructuring. "Product manager at one specific fintech" does not. Your direction stays fixed. Your titles stay flexible.
  2. Run a personal skills audit. Take one honest hour and make three lists. First, the skills people already pay you for: not what your CV says, but what colleagues actually come to you for. Second, the skills your chosen problems will demand in five years. Third, the gap between the two. Then apply one hard test to everything on list one: could you do it under pressure, in front of a stranger, and point to evidence afterwards? If not, it's an interest, not yet a skill.
  3. Check your list against the market. Spend an evening reading twenty job adverts for roles that touch your chosen problems, whether in Lagos, Nairobi, Johannesburg, or remote. Don't read them as applications. Read them as market data. Which skills appear again and again? The same WEF report finds analytical thinking remains the top core skill, called essential by seven in ten employers, followed by resilience, flexibility and agility. Our guide to digital skills that actually pay is a good cross-check for what you find.
  4. Pick one 90-day skill bet. Not five. One. Choose the single gap that would most increase your value, and give it a 90-day cycle with a concrete finish line: "by October I can build a working dashboard from raw sales data," not "learn analytics." Ninety days is the sweet spot. A year is too long to stay honest. A week is too short to build anything. One quarter is long enough to get visibly better and short enough that a wrong bet costs you three months, not a decade.
  5. Build proof, not just knowledge. Certificates say you attended. Proof says you can deliver. End every cycle with something a stranger can inspect: a dashboard built on real data, a published article, a small automation for a neighbourhood business, a talk at a local meetup. Then tell people what you built. Proof travels through relationships, and as we explain in our piece on the hidden job market, your network finds jobs before job boards do.
  6. Review and re-aim. On day 90, sit down for one hour. What did you finish? What did the market teach you? Has your problem sentence changed? Then choose the next bet. This is the step most people skip, and it's the one that makes the plan survive change. You correct course four times a year instead of watching a ten-year plan quietly expire.

Title plan versus skills plan, side by side

QuestionTitle-based planSkills-based plan
What you aim atOne specific job titleProblems you can be paid to solve
Planning rhythmFive to ten years, rarely revisited90-day cycles inside one long direction
When the market shiftsThe plan snapsThe plan re-aims
How you measure progressPromotions receivedSkills gained, proof produced, people who can vouch for you
Who owns the outcomeYour employerYou

Your first cycle starts this week

You don't need a new year or a new job to begin. You need one hour for the skills audit, one evening with those job adverts, and one bet you can finish in 90 days.

And when the plan works and a new role arrives, keep the rhythm. The same 90-day discipline is exactly how you turn your first 90 days in a new job into your next block of career capital.

Wanjiru's ten-year plan died in a restructuring memo. Her career didn't, because she had stopped building a ladder and started building a toolkit. Titles will keep appearing, merging, and vanishing. The person with a growing stock of skills, proof, and relationships will always have somewhere to stand.
